# @zakkster/lite-scheduler v1.1.1

> One package, two independent zero-GC schedulers. `createScheduler` is a
> MessageChannel-driven frame-budget manager with 5 strict priority lanes for
> browser/UI work. `FastBitScheduler` is a pure O(1) 32-tier priority queue over
> integer handles for engines and ECS. They share no code; import one and the
> other tree-shakes away (`sideEffects: false`).

Two members, one file, one intellectual lineage -- pick the one that fits:

1. Reach for `createScheduler` when you have a continuous stream of background
   work (animation, particle systems, lazy hydration, background fetches) AND
   user input that must stay responsive (taps, gestures, scroll). It owns TIME:
   a MessageChannel wakeup, a per-flush `budgetMs`, cooperative yielding.
2. Reach for `FastBitScheduler` when you already live in SoA/handle land (a game
   loop, an ECS, an audio-voice pool) and want "pop the highest-priority handle"
   in constant time with zero allocation. It is pure DATA -- no time, no
   macrotask -- so you pair it with the frame scheduler (or rAF) for a clock.

The browser provides `queueMicrotask`, `setTimeout(0)`, and
`requestAnimationFrame` -- none of which support priority. DIY priority
(setTimeout + binary heap) pays a per-priority-shift latency the frame scheduler
avoids; see Headline performance for the measured number.

## Member 1: createScheduler (the frame-budget manager)

```ts
import { createScheduler, Priority, CapacityError } from '@zakkster/lite-scheduler';

const sched = createScheduler({
  maxTasks: 2048,           // initial SLL pool size (positive int)
  budgetMs: 10,             // ms per flush before yielding (> 0)
  onCapacityExceeded: 'throw',  // 'throw' | 'grow' | 'drop'
  onError: console.error,
});

// Priority lanes -- listed strictly in execution order:
Priority.Immediate   = 0   // bypasses budget; FIFO ring buffer
Priority.UserInput   = 1   // highest SLL lane
Priority.Normal      = 2   // default
Priority.Background  = 3
Priority.Idle        = 4   // lowest

// Operations:
sched.schedule(fn, priority?);     // O(1); silent no-op after destroy
sched.shouldYield(): boolean;      // true if past budget for this flush
sched.isBusy(): boolean;           // any pending work?
sched.yieldTask(priority?): Promise<void>;
sched.stats(): { activeSllTasks, activeImmediateTasks, poolCapacity,
                 immediateCapacity, totalExecuted };
sched.destroy();                   // idempotent; closes MessageChannel

// Convenience module-level functions for a lazy-init default scheduler:
import { schedule, shouldYield, yieldTask, setDefaultScheduler } from '@zakkster/lite-scheduler';
schedule(fn, Priority.UserInput);

// Package version:
import { VERSION } from '@zakkster/lite-scheduler'; // "1.1.1"
```

### Key invariants

- All 5 priorities are honored strictly: every UserInput drains before any
  Normal; every Normal before any Background; every Background before any Idle.
- Immediate tasks bypass both the priority lanes AND the frame budget.
- Tasks scheduled DURING a flush are picked up either in the same flush (if
  budget remains) or the next macrotask. None are lost.
- `shouldYield()` returns `true` outside an active flush -- by design.
- Cancellation is intentionally not provided. Use the captured-flag pattern.
- Sync task errors -> `onError`. Async errors (rejected promises returned from
  `fn`) are NOT observed; wrap async logic in try/catch yourself.
- `destroy()` is irreversible. After destroy: `schedule()` no-ops,
  `yieldTask()` rejects, `isBusy()` returns `false`.
- Any priority that is not an integer in [UserInput..Idle] -- NaN, a fraction,
  Infinity, a string, out of range -- is coerced to Normal. Immediate (0) is
  matched exactly, before coercion.
- schedule(fn) throws a TypeError when fn is not a function (at the call site,
  not at flush time).
- An unknown config key is an error at construction, with the nearest known key
  named; onError must be callable when provided.

## Member 2: FastBitScheduler (the pure priority queue)

A 32-tier bucket priority queue over non-negative Int32 HANDLES, with an O(1)
routing mask -- "pop the highest priority" is a lowest-set-bit on a single 32-bit
int (two instructions: `x & -x`, then `Math.clz32`), no scan, however many tiers
are live. It is the package's second member; it and the frame scheduler above
never reference each other (decisions/0002), and a consumer importing only one of
them tree-shakes the other away (`sideEffects: false`).

```ts
import { FastBitScheduler, EMPTY } from '@zakkster/lite-scheduler';

const q = new FastBitScheduler(
  1024,   // capacityPerTier: ring slots per tier, integer 1..16777216 (2**24); rounds up to a power of two
  32      // numTiers: priority tiers, integer 2..32 (default 32)
);

q.push(handle, priority);   // O(1); handle is a non-negative Int32; priority 0..numTiers-1 (0 highest)
q.popMin();                 // O(1); highest-priority handle, or EMPTY (-1) when empty
q.peekMin();                // O(1); next handle without removing it, or EMPTY
q.peekPriority();           // O(1); tier of the next pop, or -1 when empty
q.isEmpty();                // O(1)
q.sizeOf(priority);         // O(1); live items in one tier (throws on a bad priority)
q.clear();                  // O(numTiers), cold; empties every tier without reallocating
q.size;                     // O(1) maintained total item count
q.capacity;                 // allocated ring capacity per tier (the round-up result)
q.requestedCapacity;        // what the caller asked for (so the round-up is observable)
q.numTiers;                 // tier count this instance was built with

// The canonical drain loop -- why EMPTY is exported:
let h; while ((h = q.popMin()) !== EMPTY) { /* use handle h */ }
```

### The handle contract

- handles are non-negative Int32 (indices into your own SoA), never objects;
- EMPTY (-1) is the ONE out-of-band value, and it is exported;
- the handle law: a stored -1 would collide with EMPTY, so push refuses it (and
  any non-integer or negative) -- which is what makes
  `while ((h = q.popMin()) !== EMPTY)` sound;
- priority is an integer 0..numTiers-1; 0 is highest; JS shift is mod 32, so an
  unchecked 32 would alias tier 0 -- it throws instead;
- a full tier throws; nothing is silently dropped;
- capacity rounds up to a power of two and the round-up is OBSERVABLE
  (capacity vs requestedCapacity);
- clear() is O(numTiers) and cold; it never reallocates;
- storage is Int32Array, never Float32Array: a float cannot represent integers
  above 2^24 exactly, so a float store would silently corrupt a large handle;
- no callbacks: the drain loop is the API (decisions/0005);
- every throw is a RangeError whose message starts `lite-scheduler:`.

### Memory (the D-07 table)

Ring storage is `capacity(rounded) * numTiers * 4` bytes (the cursor columns
heads/tails/counts add numTiers * 4 * 3 more, e.g. 384 bytes at numTiers 32):

| capacityPerTier | numTiers | bytes (buckets) | note |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1024 | 32 | 131072 | the draft's default: 128 KiB |
| 1024 | 8 | 32768 | 4x smaller for an 8-lane consumer |
| 1024 | 4 | 16384 | |
| 256 | 32 | 32768 | |
| 16777216 | 32 | 2147483648 | the documented ceiling, 2 GiB -- why the capacity door names it |

## Composability: one clock, one router

FastBitScheduler is pure data; the frame scheduler owns time. Pair them: route
handles by tier with FastBitScheduler, drain within budget under the frame
scheduler. Store the arena/SoA slot INDEX (always >= 0), never a generational
handle (which can go negative); validate liveness on pop -- that liveness check
IS the zero-alloc cancellation pattern (a "cancel" bumps a generation; the pop
skips a dead index; no token is ever allocated). See the README Composability
section for the full runnable lite-arena -> FastBitScheduler -> frame pipeline.

## Files

- [README.md](README.md): Full documentation with mermaid diagrams, the two
  quick-starts, the handle contract, the Composability pipeline, Benchmarks,
  and the design records distilled. Start here.
- [./Scheduler.js](./Scheduler.js): The implementation (both members, MIT, ESM).
- [./Scheduler.d.ts](./Scheduler.d.ts): TypeScript definitions (both members).
- [test/Scheduler.test.js](test/Scheduler.test.js): 57 node:test assertions for
  the frame scheduler -- config validation, priority semantics, capacity
  policies, the "lost work" regression, and immediate ring buffer wraparound.
- [test/FastBitScheduler.test.js](test/FastBitScheduler.test.js): 44 node:test
  cases for the second member -- every door (item, capacity, numTiers, sizeOf),
  the full surface, the tier-31 sign bit, and the fill/throw/drain regression.
- [test/dts-drift.test.js](test/dts-drift.test.js): 14 node:test surface-drift
  guards -- version parity, both-member member parity in both directions, each
  with a mutation control.
- [test/docs.test.js](test/docs.test.js): 7 hermetic doc guards -- spine order,
  relative links, ASCII, advertised-scripts-exist, provenance stamps.
- decisions/0002-dual-family, 0003-storage, 0004-tiers, 0005-no-callbacks
  (repo-only): the F2 design records for the second member.
- [bench/bench.js](bench/bench.js): 6-strategy comparison harness vs
  setTimeout, queueMicrotask, raw MessageChannel, setTimeout+heap PQ, and
  a pared-down React-scheduler clone.
- [example/demo.html](example/demo.html): Side-by-side interactive demo
  showing input latency under background load -- lite-scheduler vs setTimeout(0).
- [example/demo-scheduler-arena.html](example/demo-scheduler-arena.html): a
  lite-arena + createScheduler particle demo, toggleable backends.

## Headline performance

Measured on node v26.3.1, darwin arm64, 2026-09-14, @zakkster/lite-scheduler
1.1.0 source. Re-run `npm run bench` for your own numbers; the ratios are stable.

Head-of-line blocking (1 high-prio task scheduled in the middle of 5,000 low-prio
CPU-burning tasks; latency from schedule to run, lower is better):

| Strategy | High-prio latency | vs lite-scheduler |
|---|---:|---:|
| **lite-scheduler** | **0.119 ms** | **1.00x** |
| react-style (heap + MC + budget) | 0.232 ms | 1.95x |
| setTimeout + heap PQ | 1.447 ms | 12.13x |
| queueMicrotask (no priority) | 10.143 ms | 85.06x |
| raw MessageChannel (no priority) | 10.089 ms | 84.61x |
| setTimeout(0) (no priority) | 11.553 ms | 96.88x |

Throughput on 10,000 no-op tasks: lite-scheduler 1.095 ms, ~9.13 M tasks/sec --
within 2x of raw MessageChannel (0.934 ms), which has no scheduling features.
Steady-state heap delta across 50,000 scheduled tasks: ~0 (pool steady state).

FastBitScheduler.popMin floor vs a naive 32-tier linear scan and a binary heap of
(priority, seq) pairs, 512 items/tier, pops/sec in M/s (higher is better):

| populated tiers | FastBit popMin | naive scan | binary heap |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1  | 32.9  | 29.3  | 20.5 |
| 2  | 42.4  | 40.0  | 31.8 |
| 8  | 100.1 | 66.1  | 26.9 |
| 32 | 120.0 | 137.0 | 20.6 |

The mask's guarantee is distribution-independent O(1). It beats the (priority,
seq) heap ~5.8x at every tier count and beats the naive scan when the lowest
populated tier is high (1..8 tiers here); the honest crossover is at 32 populated
tiers, where tier 0 is always live so the scan short-circuits immediately and
edges the mask (0.88x). See the README Benchmarks section.

## When NOT to use this

- You only have one type of work -- no priority needed. Use `queueMicrotask`
  or `setTimeout` directly.
- Your work must be aligned with paint timing. Use `requestAnimationFrame`.
- You need cancellable tasks with token APIs. Use `AbortController` or
  build a thin wrapper that checks `signal.aborted` inside the task body.
- You're in a Worker that doesn't need priority. Workers serialize work
  naturally; the priority abstraction may be overkill.
- (FastBitScheduler) your items are closures or objects, not integer handles;
  or you need the queue to wake itself on a timer -- it is pure data, it never
  wakes up on its own. Pair it with a clock.
- (FastBitScheduler) you need more than 32 priority tiers -- the routing mask is
  a single 32-bit int, so 32 is the hard ceiling.

## Sibling packages

Part of the `@zakkster/*` zero-GC ecosystem:

- `@zakkster/lite-signal` -- reactive graph
- `@zakkster/lite-arena` -- ECS with generational handles + SoA sparse sets
- `@zakkster/lite-batch-buffer` -- pre-allocated WebGL vertex buffer

All compose cleanly: the scheduler drives the frame, lite-arena manages entity
state, lite-batch-buffer streams vertices to the GPU, lite-signal coordinates
state changes. Together they fit comfortably in Twitch's 1 MB / 3 s extension
budget.
